item.title: This was a triumph. I'm making a note here: huge success.
item.content:encoded:
It's hard to overstate my satisfaction. By my calculations a three-four vote margin that decided this1, which is closer than I've ever seen in a contest.

To Team Basic
 

Told ya so. Alright it was closer than my bravado may've suggested but still! In a more serious vein though: I love collaborating with other authors because it teaches me a little more about writing every time. And there aren't many better folk to learn from on the site than Roget, LurkD, and Kaktus.

LurkD, your concept was spot on. Best time I've had with writing in a while, by the way. You put together a fun team and I'm glad we weren't afraid to have a little bit of fun while creating a story. Hello World was the foundation for everything we built. There's nothing better for me than being able to write while knowing exactly where the story is headed. That's all you.

Roget you're approaching 200 articles on the site and not slowing down for anyone (nor should you). Sorry your appendix betraying you cut short your work on the AAR but it was great to work with you again, and I hope we get a chance to work together again in the future. Loved the ramblin' Hatbot in the MCF document. And I still felt connected with the main author of the proposal, he felt like a real person when I read it. Great work.

Kaktus! We finally worked together on something beyond audio! That SCP was great and still makes me laugh. I think "and that's just… so goddamned inconvenient" will stick with me for a while. Just a great great line, and still perfectly in line with the voice of the character you were portraying. You ideas for improving our stories and the path the project should take were invaluable.

To the other contestants
 

I haven't gotten around to reading very many other contest entries yet, and I really should get on that. I will say that everyone who posted content for the contest should feel proud. This is the kind of thing that helps expand the site's lore in strange and wondrous ways.

Kalinin, Von Pincier, minmin, and Zyn: You guys scared me. The sheer concentration of writing skill in your team could probably make almost anything look good but your concepts were out of this world. And then you did what I expected and executed it flawlessly. Great work, and I hope you never ever feel bad about a loss this close. You're winners in all but name.

To the organizers and judges
 

Work work and more work. Without it we'd have no contest and none of the great content that comes along with it. Decibelle: Don't stress out over the little things. You did a great job, and will continue to do a great job going forward. TroyL: Thank you for helping make this a reality. I've been waiting for a group contest ever since I just missed the last one.

Judges: Thanks for reading our shit. Back when I judged a contest with just one entry per contestant it was difficult to find the time to get to everything, you folk had way more reading to do and got it done in a timely manner. And thank you for the kind words.

To the readers
 

Thanks for taking the time. I'm glad you liked it. Now. Go write something.

Footnotes
1. Either 3 more upvotes to Rho-19 or 4 more downvotes to Kappa-10 would've shifted the averages to be a tie.

Mother of a fucking flagship. Guys, we did it.
Somewhere along the line I went from being a last-thought fourth member in a Foundation parody of the Suicide Squad to Captain of a group of three, and man, did we ever have hurdles to jump through- both irl and on-site. But just like I said every time we weren't sure we would make it- we did it. We got our entries in and we fucking punched that fish out of the water. I'm so proud to have been teammates with you two, Silber and Vince, and I can't wait to see where this MTF is going in the future. We have a lot more time to think it out now. ; )

for Deci
no go away words

Deciballerina, I know this was literal hell to set up and work through, but you did it and I am so happy for you. I know it was stressful (and I know our team certainly didn't make it any easier!) but I am incredibly proud of you and all the work you did to keep this running. I'm so grateful to have someone like you to look up to, Deci. Thank you for all that you do. <3

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I've got to give mad props to psul for his role with the team as well. It was all people's visions building on people's visions. It may have started with OMG canon, but psul came up with the framework and characterizations of Eta-11, Smapti and CumaeanSibyl grew it out, and we all ended up on the same wavelength in pulling the themes of the pieces together. CumaeanSibyl was drafting about how Hennessey wanted to stop 2402 from bringing Zoe back to a painful life, just at the same time I was drafting Hennessey learning to deal with his own death from failure and return. We all just knew what had to be said.

Well, like I said in the OMG canon, when it's time for an idea, it comes.

And Deci and Troy, thank you for pulling this together! Judging all the works and managing the contest is not easy.

Everyone who participated, you should feel proud. There's a whole lot of new material, new ideas, new storylines, new characters, just the amount of worldbuilding that's been done in the past month has been phenomenal. Congrats to Team Basic for the win, and congrats to everyone to making the Foundation a greater, more beautiful, more detailed place to exist.

item.title: EXUBERANT SCREECH

Kal, Pincier, min, you guys are the best. :D

Kalinin, it was your vision that brought all this about. We wouldn't have had a story without you, and I remember all of the chat discussions we had about writing were all super exciting. I remember being really excited throughout pretty much the entire process of this, really.

item.title: ONE VOTE MORE

You forgot to mention your own credit, for contributing most of the content (and having it be quality content, though that goes without saying), not to mention the core idea pitch in the first place.

To Zyn, you essentially wrote the entirety of the human character side of our entries, and half the non-human ones too! Everything would certainly have been way more dry without your contributions. And your entry is the cutest thing I've read onsite all year!

And Pincier, I'll admit I'm not the biggest fan of the Church, but the solid brainstorming sessions with you, as well as your amazing GOI format article, have definitely sold me on the theology. Who knows, the stuff you contributed to this just might make clockworks cool again. :D

The results are a little disappointing - I knew I should have pimped this more in chat - but mostly very satisfying. I'm glad to have worked with y'all to produce something we can all be proud of making.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
There's not much else I can say that Ty and sirpudding haven't already captured. I still want to say though - congratulations. To everyone, not just the winners. Just like the GOI contest helped open our minds to write worlds where the other players in the Foundationverse(s) were more than simple friends or enemies but real people1, you've all kickstarted something great once more. You've expanded the universe again to explore the men and women with boots on the ground. And you've done so with a hell of a lot of creativity, ingenuity, and elbow grease. All of you have something to be proud of.

I too wish to thank my teammates.

+ Sirpudding
- Master of realism

Sirpudding forced us to go the extra mile for realism and coherence where we could, which showed and drastically improved our work. He also constantly strove to lead by example and took the initiative to create and introduce ideas that absolutely made the storyline. But more than that, sirpudding was flexible. Far more than I would've been in his place, and I envy that quality.

When I posted Avatara, it forced him to make changes to his planned AAR - but he did so happily and not only found a way to retcon Avatara with the realism he desired, but add more versimilitude, even more exciting tidbits, and introduce many more interesting perspectives on our storyline.

From the outstandingly cool Hellgate Point Defense System to Crow Far-Walker's indignant explanation of who really stole the fire, sirpudding consistently came up with excellent little details and fought to maintain a constant standard of quality in all of our works. In doing so, he proved that the devil truly is in the details.

Thank you sirpudding, for bringing your experience, imagination, and flexibility to the team.

+ GreenWolf
- Long-suffering technical wizard

Ask GreenWolf and he'll tell you he did barely anything. Ask anyone else and they'll tell you that GreenWolf has not only done more for Prometheus Labs than anyone alive but has helped bring it into the modern era kicking and screaming. He's introduced new themes, new branches, and new science fiction aspects that at once seem so obvious and so brilliantly ingenious.

Naturally, GreenWolf did the same in the contest, this time using his trademark scientific versimilitude to create a story where Prometheus Labs quite literally stole the power of the Gods. He nailed down the science of the science fiction both in the story and real life.

In real life, GreenWolf was our omnipresent technical wizard, using his arcane knowledge of Wikidot and 'computer programming'2 to make our lives infinitely easier, from teaching me how to create the page offset that made Samsara's endings possible to whipping up his own chatbot for use in the team discussion chatroom.

Thank you, GreenWolf, for being a technical and scientific savant, both in your stories and real life.

+ TyGently
- Second-in-command and real captain

When GreenWolf first brought TyGently aboard the team I was secretly hesitant; when the next contest starts you can be damn sure I'll the the first one knocking at his door. TyGently stayed up at all hours of the night3 to envision a story of gods, men, and monsters all being drawn inexplicably to their destiny, and then slap us in the face with it so that all we could do was say "I like Ty's story. Let's use his story."

Ty had arguably one of the hardest entries to write (whoever says SCPs are easy has clearly never written one) and tackled it with gusto, creating a compelling character as well as a story of revenge, forgiveness, and finding one's place in the world. All I did was wrangle us into place, while he plotted out the path to take and then led us down that path with ease.

In Samsara, TyGently had the odious task of bringing five different characters together for a climactic confrontation, characterizing a major player for the first time in the entire storyline, and then creating endings that brought the arc to a compelling yet satisfying close no matter which one was chosen. And he pulled it off - not only that, but actually brought tears to readers' eyes.

Thank you, TyGently, for creating a compelling storyline and compelling characters.

Footnotes
1. Shoutout to Clef's GOC canon which came before
2. magic probably
3. and probably irreparably wrecked his health

item.title: Re: Judge Comments
item.content:encoded: Yeah, I have read that article, but really I chose the name independent of that, there's no connection intended. The name isn't uncommon, I have known a few Israfils and Israels personally, and the association with the herald of the apocalypse is, as you say, probably the common thread between the two uses.

item.title: Re: Judge Comments
item.content:encoded:
I honestly have no idea why this was eyebrow-raising, or which "Israfil" I am thought to be referencing here

I assume it was interpreted as a reference to Action 10-Israfil in SCP-579. I didn't register that name when reading, and of course the likelihood is that there is a common origin (names indicating a herald of the apocalypse) rather than one causing the other.

item.title: Re: Judge Comments
item.content:encoded:
As an aside, evoking Israfil was an eyebrow-raising choice that served no apparent purpose beyond namedropping, but which did no real harm to the work as a whole.

I honestly have no idea why this was eyebrow-raising, or which "Israfil" I am thought to be referencing here; I chose the name because it is an Arabic name, and probably not uncommon in 10th century Morocco or Córdoba and also because of the association with the Quaranic angel who heralds the apocalypse. It shouldn't be raising any more eyebrows than if I named him "Jibril" or "Khalid".

+ spoilers
– hide block

Now it is true that Israfil's story doesn't match that of SCP-2970 or even other accounts within The Lord of Endowments (even Rashid, ostensibly a follower of de Guzman, calls him out), and this was a happy accident stemming initially from an error on my part, that I developed into a deliberately unreliable narrator, both because the Serpent's Hand format, I feel, benefits from ambiguity and because when I asked myself why he would lie I got some interesting answers. The reader is invited to do so as well.

Was this what was meant?

item.title: Re: Contest Totals!
item.content:encoded:
I don't think it was the presentation necessarily. As I pointed out on multiple occasions, the presentation works against it most of the time, limiting the ability to describe the world and undercutting some of the action with silly effects.

More likely, I just think the explanation is just that many audiences enjoy these kinds of stories, regardless of the tropes.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
A round of applause to Team Basic - it was a high standard contest, and it took a high standard to win it.

Many congratulations to everyone who participated and submitted entries - you are excellent for doing so, and you should feel excellent. I have thoroughly enjoyed reading the wide scope of submissions - from cyberspace to Venus to dreamscapes to the Almerían desert, this was a contest that allowed creativity to shine through. Although, if there was a theme to the winning teams, it was the quest for the divine, and what that means when it is undertaken by innocents, rather than those with baser motives.

A huge thank-you to everyone who acted as judges. It is a difficult and sometimes under-appreciated role, but the contest couldn't happen without you - we really value your time, thought and feedback.

Speaking of people who the contest couldn't happen without: thanks again to Decibelle and Troy. I enjoyed my first team contest enormously, and a lot of that was down to the way it was conceived.

Of course, most of my enjoyment was from the great teammates. I've tried to express this in my comments on your entries (which I will now be upvoting furiously!), but thank you - I have learned a lot about writing from working with you, and I'm very grateful for the opportunity.

item.title: Judge Comments
item.content:encoded:
Following are selected comments from the judges, both positive and negative. Judges are not required to reveal their identity, quotes, or anything else unless they choose to do so. These comments were passed along by the judges for the benefit of the teams involved in the contest.

Long Live The Cake! (“Chi-17”)

Credit to the focus on a single event over multiple long pieces.

It is always nice to see people from other branches compete in these contests, especially in a team setting. There was some groundwork for some interesting ideas, and if proofread more and updated for some more originality, this could be a very entertaining MTF. It wouldn't be too hard for other authors to adapt this MTF into their own work.

I think I could've given more points if it wasn't so difficult to read. I did like the original images, though.

To varying degrees, all of the submissions in this set were inescapably distracting due to writing issues. Purple prose, serious grammatical flaws, flow and structure issues, and a hell of a lot of unneeded verbosity about tactical details and other minutia with very little impact on the narrative.

Technical Support (“Rho-9”)

The various entries work together to form a clear, interesting MTF. The concept is very distinct and well explained, and it fills an unoccupied niche. I loved the Redzone Security article for being a believable snapshot of some of the less dramatic parts of containment. Special note goes to the text adventure. Is it gimmicky? Yes. But that gimmick in itself works to support the theme of the MTF. I like when form reinforces theme.

I enjoy the idea of an MTF who function as tech support for anomalous technology. Overall though, the execution felt off and not too engaging, save for a couple entries. The risk in making a CYOA and the AAR being in a unique way was nice to see, but it fell short of what it aimed for and could accomplish. This would be an MTF other authors could easily accommodate into their work.

Overall, I feel that these generally didn't go far enough. Decent, but not written to their full potential.

As someone with a background in software, I ended up liking these entries a lot more than the general population seems to have. The CVE format of the first document was an effective and well-realized hook; all the more unfortunate that it’s proven too dry for persons in other disciplines. The unix meme-dodging puzzle was inventive and entertaining, arguably because of the dead ends rather than in spite of them (though having to restart from scratch each time got a bit tedious quick). Things get a little over the top in places, and the complaints that there isn’t much narrative are well founded, but overall I’m very pleased with this submission.

We’re Here Too (“Lambda-5”)

The multidimensional murder of a specific group of people. Can’t say I’ve seen that before. The SCP was, in my opinion, excellent. Especially conceptually. The actual reason behind the bodies was a letdown. Leaving it as a mystery would ultimately have been more interesting. Stories had bad pacing. Nice to see some queen stuff, even if it is a little odd in form.

There were some good ideas here, and while there wasn't anything groundbreaking happening, the material produced was decent. Where this team really fell flat was not tying up the story in a clean way to produce a satisfying read, even if the overall material was good. While the MTF could be adaptable by other authors, the narrow-minded focus brought in these stories would make it hard for other authors to use them.

I liked the semi-twist revealed in the last Tale.

I had a hard time telling which of the works was the after-action report; I assume it was the supplemental interview to the SCP, but none of them quite made sense. The exposition is also not as well spread-out as I’d like; we have a lot of “what” spread out among the various articles, but the “why” all comes in one lump sum in the last piece, which is not strong enough to close out on what was built up elsewhere. Overall, good ideas and build up, but weak conclusions.

Site-19 String Quartet (“Eta-11”)

This is my favorite MTF in the contest. Good, direct concept and characterization. It fulfills a role that’s perhaps been seen before, but with a very distinct spin. The characters in it actually feel like people, distinct from their job identities. Props to psul for writing some superb tales.

While not entirely ambitious, the focus of the entire team and their dedication to a coherent story is impressive and very well-done. Both the SCP and GoI Format articles were good. Indeed, the SCP this team has produced is one of the only ones (in my opinion) that did not serve only as a vehicle for the other entries. However, neither were as on-point as the tales/recovery document, which seamlessly included material from all eras of the site to clearly define what this MTF is and could do. This is an easily adaptable MTF for other authors to use.

Very nice expansion on existing auditory SCPs, as well as furthering the Mount Golgotha Tale series.

I don’t think I’d ever read 012 prior to reviewing this submission. For such a sparse source, there’s quite a bit of interesting buildup around this skip, even prior to this contest, and the additional mythos that’s been added around it here is compelling. Indeed, this whole work integrates remarkably well with existing content across the board. While I find myself disappointed in the lack of closure regarding the initial conceit (the theft of 012), I’m overall very pleased with these submissions, both in the context of the contest and in the larger contribution to the site.

Apotheosis (Tau-5, “Samsara”)

I wasn’t sold at first, but these stories do a fantastic job of coming together to form a whole picture. The SCP entry was interesting, but perhaps not as distinct as it could have been. This may be a natural consequence of the majority of its story being contained within other entries. This entry tells a sweeping story through multiple different entries. No one entry revealed everything, but taken as a whole, an impressive story is revealed.

This team married science fiction with fantasy to produce an entertaining storyline with very well-written characters. While the storyline felt a bit disjointed at times and didn't always entertain, it was still clear the team not only tried their hardest to create something unique for both the universe their MTF is in and the GOIs used, but succeeded. Nanku's sudden "death" in "Avatara" was one of the rare moments in the contest that I had to do a double-take out of surprise, and it still has stuck with me. Given the setting the storyline is in, it could be hard to use this MTF, but the scope is decently sized to where I can see new ground being made with them.

The voice/viewpoint of the Samsara people was very well done.

On the one hand, I don’t feel like I came away with a clear, explicit idea of what the Samsara project is about from the Foundation’s perspective. On the other, the underlying ideas- which were far more important to the narrative- are extremely well developed and explored, forming a rich narrative that I deeply enjoyed. The Foundation itself is largely in the background on this one, but given the highly unorthodox nature of the given MTF, that works in the story’s favor.
As an aside, evoking Israfil was an eyebrow-raising choice that served no apparent purpose beyond namedropping, but which did no real harm to the work as a whole.

There’s No Me In Team (“Mu-3”)

Not a bad effort, but both a more unique MTF concept and a more engaging SCP concept would help immensely.

There wasn't much sense of direction that I could find here. Though there was a clear path this wanted to take, it didn't seem to be traveled in a way to hold my attention well. While it's fine that both the SCP and GoI Format played off of each other to document the same anomaly, the SCP ultimately wasn't as interesting as the GoI Format. However, I can see this MTF being adaptable into other works in the future and deliver more depth into the dynamic of MC&D and the Foundation.

Marshal, Carter, and Dark is a less ambitious scope compared to many of the other entries, and it led to a fairly dry narrative with fairly little substance despite its considerable length. What’s left is largely a run-of-the-mill espionage story that does very little to differentiate itself.

The Dream Team

Some very good stuff, held back by a need for clarity. I’d personally have found it more interesting were the foundation trying to research and understand all this from a more external perspective. We are given many systems and terms that operate with an internal logic unknown to the reader. That can be good, but here, it overwhelms.

This team, more than any of the others in this contest, pushed themselves to create some of the most inventine work of the contest by taking ideas and concepts explored before in new and weird directions. The dream logic persistent throughout, even in a dry, clinical SCP, made it necessary to examine and reflect on each entry deeply, almost always rewarding the reader. It also helped make an underused GoI like Oneiroi more interesting by exploring just how the Foundation interacts with it. My biggest issue is that the team didn't explore ways to include other tales or skips into their work and flesh it out even more. While this MTF isn't too easily adaptable by others, I can envision ways people might use them to positive effect.

The portrait of the dreamscape and everything that surrounds it painted here is astounding. An exceptional amount of work was clearly put into both the documents and the worldbuilding behind them. Easily my favorite of the first half of the submissions.

A Slow but Steady Increase in the Number of Games in Town (Sigma-66, “Sixteen Tons”)

The actual plot wasn’t bad, but the characterization was overdone. They were not believable people. Just not much to distinguish this one, I’m afraid.

Fun. That's the word that best describes this team's entries. Not every entry was executed well, but they managed to be consistently enjoyable. While not too original, it's very reminiscent of comic books, and pulled off with enough humor and self-awareness to overcome otherwise questionable moments of implausibility and weakness. However, the entries are overall not particularly strong and could do with further expansion outside of the contest by the authors involved. "MTF Sigma-66 Post-Mission Psychological Evaluation" is my favorite AAR of the contest. This is an MTF that could be relatively simple to adapt, though it might be tricky to pull off given the unusual way this MTF is set up to begin with.

Of the various concepts that have come up in this contest, “GOI Suicide Squad” that caught me off guard for some reason. The elements of absurdism are restrained but add a lot of flavor and a little comic relief to an otherwise dark concept. There’s fairly little narrative, and the themes aren’t much explored past face value, but the work is competent and sets up a framework I’d enjoy seeing more of.

We Deny The Existence of Other Games In Town (Sigma-3, “The Bibliographers”)

A top quality entry. Perhaps the best entry for expanding the foundation itself.

The dynamic between the Foundation and The Wanderer's Library, explored via this MTF, was pulled off in an enjoyable and engaging way. The use of a CYOA embedded in an SCP for an after-action report and in a GoI Format is pretty damn creative, and the multiple paths it gives made it one of the stronger AARs of the contest. The inclusion of the Library as a setting piece for all the work was done in a positive way, and the way the two orientations played off of each other worked well. The Navarro tales were also a highlight for me. I only really wish the team was more ambitious in being original (CYOA's are not enough in that regard) and that there was more of a coherent and arching story beyond showing us individual situations this MTF got involved in (the closest we came were Lessons Learned and the two orientations). This is an adaptable MTF, and one authors could easily use and work into stories about the Hand and/or the Library.

There’s a pretty slow build up in this collection, and a lot of it is self-justification and exposition. The self-justification in particular is understandable given the views of the old guard, and surprisingly well done in some of the later instances. At the same time, it feels a little forced and is perhaps even dated in light of a modern site culture that’s embraced far more unconventional ideas in this contest. Additionally, the sheer enormity of the work is intimidating to the point of archive shock, which I fear may prove a stumbling block to future readers. All of that aside, I enjoyed Sigma 3, particularly in its impressive consolidation of ideas that have become vitally important to the site’s meta but have previously been challenging to track down. While I don’t believe that this was the strongest submission to the contest, I do believe it to be the most constructive addition to the site’s core mythos by a large margin.

The Notos Blues & Jazz Band Experience (“Rho-19”)

Tells a traditional story, but does it pretty damn well. Volume 19.113.A-01 gets props for embracing the technoreligious nature of its GoI.

This team's works were written near-perfectly and produced some of the best work in the contest by far. In almost all areas, the team succeeded. It was hard to rank this team on originality, as they did some very awesome things with what they setting. What keeps them from ranking higher in this area is that, much like "A Slow but Steady Increase", this feels like a very faithful homage but to science fiction. And just being set in the future and steeped deep into sci-fi isn't enough to make it fully original in the SCPverse. I also wish the inclusions/references to other SCPs were more fleshed-out than vague references. Otherwise, this team did a spectacular job. This MTF doesn't seem usable anymore, given how the story went, and would probably need extensive retooling to work outside of the context of this storyline.

The narrative and novel near-future setting presented here is fascinating and deeply engaging, and I enjoyed it a great deal. The MTF described has a much more finite focus and objective than many others, but I think that worked very well both for the contest and for the story here told. While I regret the loss of the team’s most interesting member as demanded by the plot, I’m hopeful that we’ll see more like him in the future.

A thoroughly traditional science fiction story. Nothing new here. But it's told in a fairly interesting, forward way within the scope of the Foundation's plot. I just wish it were possible for other people to actually expand on what's been given.

Team Basic (“Kappa-10”)

Excellent use of alternative formats and mixed media. Perhaps the biggest strength of the story. Very high production values in this one. An interesting story thoroughly devoted to the AI theme.

Hatbot. Of all the fucking things to expand on. Hatbot.

The work here was consistently fun and, even at its most predictable, still managed to surprise and entertain in multiple ways. Bringing in a little-used group (the Manna Charitable Foundation) and making them intertwine with their storyline and even other GoIs helped bring out the group's dynamic between their setting and characters. The usage of an old and (somewhat) inside-joke to turn it into something serious was a bold move that paid off well, and incorporating it all into their past canon and highlighting the best of all the different GoIs helped make this a strong, story-based experience. The only downside is that I wish it took more risks and went more out-there with its genre and setting; this would have turned the series into as memorable a classic as any series. This MTF could be pretty well-adapted into other settings, given enough author creativity.

I’ve only seen bits and pieces of the AI series that serves as the background for this entry, and almost nothing of Maxwellism beyond the original Xbox bros, but the results were a lot of fun. The unique format allows the members of Kappa-10 to make very strong impressions of character and personality at no cost to storytelling. Expanding on what I believe to be old site RP lore regarding the antagonist (or possibly, just the immortalization of a meme as an SCP) was an especially fun touch.

As a final note, this is the closest contest I've ever been involved with on the site. TroyL and I double-checked the math a few times just to verify. It's close enough that I could almost call this one a tie. Really, in the community vote, the .5 (which was double checked by me thrice) was enough to swing the vote entirely. Never let it be said that one member's vote can't change the outcome of a contest, because this time, it did.

Congratulations to all involved. The official winners are:

First place, Team Basic ("Kappa-10").

Second place, The Notos Blues & Jazz Band Experience ("Rho-19").

Third place, Apotheosis (Tau-5, "Samsara").

Thank you all for participating! It was lovely to see all the entries, and I'm really proud of every team that competed! Stay tuned for quotes from the judges, posted by TroyL. And remember; every single vote in a contest counts, as we can very clearly see right here.

The Lord of Endowments actually came about rather organically. I had put the escaping wizard into Operation AZURE PEREGRINE primarily to keep the mission from being an unqualified success. item.title: Contest review
item.content:encoded:
Having now read all of the contest entries, I also wanted to say how impressed I have been at the standard generally. There have been a range of approaches to the contest criteria, which I think speaks to both the strength of the writing community, and also a well-conceived contest allowing for versatility.

+ My thoughts on winning teams
- For what they're worth

As a way of consolidating my thoughts, I ran through the entries again, scoring them on the following basis:

  • Each entry was given a score out of ten.
  • Each team was then scored only for the 5 highest-scoring articles that satisfied the competition criteria. For example, teams with more than two tales would have the two highest scoring tales included, but if the third tale scored higher than their SCP article, the third tale would still be excluded, as the SCP article would be necessary to meet the entry criteria.
  • On top of the per-article scores, I gave a mark out of ten for "story", and a mark out of twenty for "MTF team" (covering the clarity of conception of the team, and the characterisation within it) - this was based on the contest introduction's suggestions of "it's time to tell their stories" and "your team will create a new MTF".
  • I scored all teams except the one I was part of (as I can't possibly be objective about that work), but I have only set out the top five teams below. I agree with others that it was pretty close across the top 7 or so teams.

Rank: 5
Team: Team Basic
Score: 48
Comments: I'd only read a little bit of AIAD before, so some of this was lost on me. Great presentation throughout, but it felt as though slightly too much time and text was spent describing things (characters, action) that were predictable. Skipping some of that, or developing the ideas/tropes further, might have helped. The two things I enjoyed the most were the non-hatbot related articles. A clear mission statement for the MTF, and a clear story arc, added to the scores.

Rank: 4
Team: We Deny The Existence of Other Games In Town
Score: 49
Comments: Some great individual articles, but they didn't quite cohere into a clear picture of how the taskforce interacted. That might have been due to the MTF's very broad remit, and the fact that the story spread tendrils in different directions, rather than keeping a tight focus. I wasn't hugely taken with the orientations, but credit to the depth of writing both there and in the twine sections. Navarro got some great character moments.

Rank: 3
Team: The Dream Team
Score: 56
Comments: Containing the best single entry in the competition (#Xiupania), this had moments where it threatened to cross over into greatness - the dream logic was palpable throughout, and Sherry and Urooj in particular developed into real characters over the course of the story. Perhaps undermined slightly in the lack of clarity (ha!) of Dr Glass, and some other stray ends, but overall a very immersive story and one that I could see being continued to good effect.

Rank:2
Team: Apotheosis
Score: 60
Comments: After the first few entries, I was quite uncertain. It was the back half of this team's work that really brought together the story and developed the characters. The use of GoI formats was natural and pushed the story along without it seeming artificial, and the climactic tale helped humanise the team, as well as providing a fitting ending (or endings).

Rank: 1
Team: The Notos Blues & Jazz Band Experience
Score: 61.5
Comments: An extremely high standard across the board, including impressively consistent work across multiple authors on the most fully-realised character in the contest (Manu-13). The story, while familiar in the broad strokes, was paced beautifully and brought to life through clever detailing of personalities and emotions. If I had a criticism, it would be that I didn't get a chance to spend more time with the backup team and get to know them better. Whether this wins or not, it deserves recognition as being amongst the best story-sequences on the site.

item.title: Re: Wherein I review the entire contest.
item.content:encoded:
This is an interesting review format! I might have to steal it, once I finish reading everything.

+ Critique Response: We Deny The Existence of Other Games In Town
– hide block
  • I'm pleased that you felt we were successful regarding Portability, as this was a very high concern for me. Most of the fun I have here is writing with stuff other people made — and that's because they made it usable in the first place.
  • I don't agree with the critique of the Twine script as the AAR — obviously — but I think you're on point with "we could've done more to show how the team works in action" and "show how the task force's structure works" (and the first person to point it out, as far as I'm aware).
    • For instance, in retrospect it's easy to conclude that there are like two dozen people in Sigma-3 max judging from the AAR, and comparing to some of the other MTFs being fairly tiny — when that was supposed to be just one team of many, given Sigma-3's particular structure. But this is never addressed directly in our material. I wish we had.
  • I'm sorry to hear that you didn't find much of it noteworthy; although your reaction is interesting in that you felt the Navarro stories carried it. The Navarro stories are the most underrated parts of our sequence, I think.
  • To be perfectly honest, we had about double the material planned compared to what was actually posted; at several points we were joking that we were the "We Got Fucked By RL" team. Of course, given the sheer number of disqualifications and last minute posting, I think many people were in the same boat. (And given the amount of text I did produce myself, I was probably personally being unrealistic.)

Thank you for your critique!

I particularly admire the effort you put into reading everyone's works. Not just as a contest participant, but as a staff member who would be super happy if more people went the extra mile like that. (A few others already have, too, and that's also awesome.)

item.title: Wherein I review the entire contest.
item.content:encoded:
I've finally finished reading all of the contest entries, I've voted on most of them (and when I haven't it was as a deliberate neutral vote) and commented on all but one or two. As a whole, this contest produced a truly surprising amount of very good work, and I'm extremely proud to have participated!

Team Reviews (note that I'm only reviewing teams that posted content):

+ Format
– hide block

Team: Team name
Entries: Number of entries by type and comments on specific entries
Qualification: Whether the team met the entry requirements (as far as I can tell) or not
Designation: MTF designation and nickname
Class: My best guess as to the classification of the team according to Mobile Task Forces
Mission: My understanding of the what the primary mission of the task force is
Portability: My assessment (from "Very Low" to "Very High") of how usable the task force is in future articles
Review: My review of the team's entries as a whole.
Rank: How I would rank the qualifying teams if it were up to me

+ Long Live the Cake!
– hide block

Team: Long Live The Cake!
Entries: 1 SCP, 1 GOI format (Chaos Insurgency), 3 tales, 1 AAR, 1 edited inclusion (translation)
Qualification: Yes
Designation: MTF Chi-7 "Pacific Force"
Class: Combat
Mission: Naval operations and forward deployment contingency operations
Portability: Average; Chi-7 can go anywhere in the world and has a pretty flexible operational portfolio (including ground, naval, and air operations), but it as a combat task force it's usefulness in SCPs and tales is more limited than containment, tracking or undercover task forces. There are also plausibility problems with the Foundation concealing the operations of a supercarrier and its task group from the public.
Review: This team's biggest problem was their poor English skills. I definitely applaud Long Live The Cake! for even attempting to enter a foreign language creative writing contest. Beyond that the team's entries focused on a story about an exchange with Chaos Insurgency Operatives, that wasn't especially interesting in and of itself. Much of the military operations were very unrealistic and their choice of the very difficult to pull off Chaos Insurgency format probably worked against them. I am surprised they didn't use the Big E more directly in their entries as she is a very distinct part of their task force concept and carries a lot of sentimental value besides.
Rank: 11th

+ Technical Support
– hide block

Team: Technical Support
Entries: 1 SCP, 1 GOI Format (Redzone), 2 tales, 1 AAR, 0 edited inclusions; this was one of four teams to use a new GOI format and the only one to use a wholly new GOI
Qualification: Yes
Designation: MTF Rho-9; I wasn't able to find a nickname if any
Class: Engineering; Rho-9 appears to be the only Engineering task force in the contest
Mission: Countermeasures and security regarding anomalous information technology
Portability: High; Articles in this team's wheelhouse are fairly common, and information technology is indirectly involved in everything the foundation does. As a engineering team they can appear in a supporting role, or as the primary operational element depending on the situation.
Review: This was a very good concept executed very lacklusterly. With the exception of Warm Milk and Ramen all of these team's entries effectively amounted to a lot of set-up with no real payoff.
Rank: 8th

+ We're here too
– hide block

Team: We're here too
Entries: 1 SCP, 1 GOI format (Black Queen), 2 tales, 1 AAR (I'm assuming the interview is being counted here), 0 edited inclusions
Qualification: Yes
Designation: Lambda-5 "White Rabbits"
Class: Containment; although I'm extremely not sure about this
Mission: Containing a specific "reality bender" (and getting killed all over the multiverse in the process)
Portability: Very Low; the main thing Lambda-5 does is get killed by Charles Hull, which can only go so far until it is boringly repetitious.
Review: This started out with a solid mystery, dead MTF operatives appearing from parallel worlds, but then just fizzled. I was especially disappointed by the twist ending of Lambda-Killer which seems to come out of left-field with absolutely no follow up to it, and The Lives of Charles Hull which is a first-person infodump monologue by the villain of the series. I get the impression that the team had some fairly ambitious plans, but just ran out of time.
Rank: 10th

+ Site-19 String Quartet
– hide block

Team: Site-19 String Quartet
Entries: 1 SCP, 1 GOI Format (Are We Cool Yet?), 4 tales, 1 AAR, 0 edited inclusions; I'm fairly surprised this team didn't have any edited inclusions as the Savage Beasts seem well suited for some of the previous work by team members. I think An Impenitent Thief was the best tale in the contest.
Qualification: Yes
Designation: MTF Eta-11 "Savage Beasts"
Class: Containment
Mission: Containing sonic anomalies
Portability: Very High; Eta-11's wheelhouse encompasses a wide variety of potential operations, and as a narrative element they were very well characterized both as an organization and as individuals, making them very easy for authors to use. They were also one of only two teams to really try to tie the new MTF into existing stories and characters (like SCP-1638 and the On Mount Golgotha canon), and I think were the more successful of the two.
Review: I was very impressed by this team's work. They primarily told a single cohesive story that covers only a few hours in a single night, and in it they very clearly established their characters and themes. The themes of duty in the face of obsolescence, loss, and the nature of silence were very well carried throughout the entire work.
Rank: 2nd

+ Apotheosis
– hide block

Team: Apotheosis
Entries: 1 SCP, 2 GOI Formats (Prometheus Labs and Serpent's Hand), 2 Tales, 1 AAR, 1 edited inclusion
Qualification: Yes
Designation: MTF Tau-5 "Samsara"
Class: Combat
Mission: Extremely hazardous operations and field testing paratech
Portability: Low; as a combat task force the uses are more limited than other types and Samsara offers two endings (of three options) that are pretty final for the MTF. Also many readers seem to have issues with the Foundation deploying transhuman operatives armed with weird science.
Review: It was really great working with Team Apotheosis, and I think we had a lot of natural synergy and simpatico. We hit the ground running already in sync, for example all of our proposed names for the team were along the same lines as "apotheosis". I can't really objectively review our work, but I think we had a really good story, that maybe wasn't as thematically cohesive as some of the other teams but had a lot of verisimilitude and tons of great world-building details. Plus I got to write about Hellgate PDS, how monkey hive-minds measure things, and name drop Coyote.
Rank: 3rd

+ There's No Me in Team
– hide block

Team: There's No Me in Team
Entries: 1 SCP, 1 GOI Format (Marshall Carter and Dark Limited), 2 tales, 2 AARs, 0 edited inclusions; this was the only team to have multiple AARs.
Qualification: Yes
Designation: MTF Mu-3 "Highest Bidders"
Class: Undercover
Mission: Covert operations in anomalous markets especially MC&D
Portability: Average; while their wheelhouse is reasonably broad the focus on MC&D is limiting. This team created a ton of organizational details which should be useful to future writers.
Review: This team's entries all focused on a single operation "Free Market". This, I feel, caused some problems for them because all of their entries repeat some of the same information. Furthermore they entered two documents, which while realistic, were rather boring, and one document that wasn't very well written at all.
Rank: 9th

+ The Dream Team
– hide block

Team: The Dream Team
Entries: 1 SCP, 1 GOI Format (Oneiroi West), 4 tales, 1 AAR; this was one of the four teams that used a brand new GOI Format. I think #Xiapania was the best GOI format in the contest.
Qualification: Yes
Designation: MTF Omicron-Rho "The Dream Team"; this was one of only two teams to break the standard Greek alphanumeric designation for MTFs.
Class: Esoteric
Mission: Oneironautic operations
Portability: Low; the realm of dreams is a very specific environment. Also this team gave nearly no details about the mechanics of oneirnautics, which will present difficulties for future use. Agent Sherry Wilson survived the attack on Qi Shao, and presumably can be used in future work.
Review: This was some of the more imaginative work in the contest, and #Xiapania is simply breathtaking. The development of the Qi Shao story-line wasn't very clearly executed, and I personally found the motives of Mr. Glass to be impossible to determine from the information we were given. The mechanics of oneironautics were barely touched on, and in much of the work the line between waking and dream states was needlessly blurred.
Rank: 4th

+ Send in the Clowns
– hide block

Team: Send in the Clowns
Entries: 2 SCPs, 1 GOI Format (Shark Punching Centre), 1 tale, 0 AARs, and 0 edited inclusions; this was one of the four teams to use a new GOI format.
Qualification: No
Designation: MTF Omicron-8 "Send in the Clowns"
Class: Containment
Mission: Containment of anomalous objects related to humor
Portability: Average; The MTF's wheelhouse is very specific, and there was clearly difficulty even in the contest of justifying their use. Specific characters as well as some idea about the organizational character of the task force was established, and could be used elsewhere.
Review: I think this team had one very impressive entry, SPC-2615, which may be the boldest successful entry in the contest and some fairly mediocre ones.
Rank: NA

+ A Slow but Steady Increase in the Number of Games in Town
– hide block

Team: A Slow but Steady Increase in the Number of Games in Town
Entries: 1 SCP, 1 GOI format (Marshall Carter and Dark Limited format-screw), 2 tales, 1 AAR (I think) and 0 edited inclusions; this was one of three teams to use a modified GOI format.
Qualification: Yes
Designation: MTF Sigma-66 "Sixteen Tons"
Class: Undercover
Mission: Former members of GOIs used for deniable covert operations
Portability: Average; these guys are a ton of fun, and they are given very distinct characterizations, but deniable operations is a fairly specific niche.
Review: This team had the most fun entries, and I was thoroughly entertained throughout. They definitely sacrificed verisimilitude for entertainment, but didn't lose my willing suspension of disbelief. I feel like the conclusion of the storyline was a bit truncated, though. My only real issue was that the concept feels very derivative of DC Comics' Suicide Squad down to the explosive collars.
Rank: 5th

+ We Deny The Existence of Other Games In Town
– hide block

Team: We Deny The Existence of Other Games In Town
Entries: 1 SCP, 1 GOI format (Serpent's Hand format-screw), 5 tales, 1 AAR, 0 edited inclusions; this was one of three teams to use a modified GOI format. The AAR here was one of two that were not at all what I expected from the contest requirements.
Qualification: Yes
Designation: MTF Sigma-3 "Bibliographers"
Class: Undercover
Mission: Running intelligence assets in the esoteric occult community
Portability: Very High; the wheelhouse is broad enough to encompass a lot of what the Foundation does, either directly or indirectly and some strong characters were included in this series as well as ton of organizational detail. This was one of two teams to try to weave the new team into existing story-lines and characters.
Review: This was largely carried by the Navarro stories and Lessons Learned, and while the rest was interesting it wasn't especially noteworthy. I don't feel the choice to use a Twine script as the AAR was a good one; I didn't get a sense of how the team works in action, or of the organizational identity and place in the Foundation's bureaucracy at all.
Rank: 6th

+ Jäeger Bombers
– hide block

Team: Jäeger Bombers
Entries: 1 SCP, 1 GOI Format (Global Occult Coalition), 1 tale, 1 AAR, no edited inclusions; this was one of four teams to use a brand new GOI format.
Qualification: No
Designation: Eta-5 "Jäeger Bombers"
Class: Combat
Mission: Neutralization of giant monsters
Portability: Low; giant monsters are only usable so far in wainscot settings and some apparently important details about this task force (like an extra-dimensional base) aren't really explored here.
Review: I was generally rather disappointed in this team's entries. There were some good ideas here, but the execution was definitely lacking.
Rank: NA

+ Team Wayfarer
– hide block

Team: Team Wayfarer
Entries: 1 SCP, 1 GOI Format (Serpent's Hand), 2 tales, 0 AARs, 0 edited inclusions
Qualification: No
Designation: MTF Eta-13 "Gulliver's Tourists"
Class: Tracking? really should be Expeditionary but that category doesn't exist; I suppose this is the only team that made a task force that needs a new class.
Mission: Exploration of the Hyrda's Spine nexus.
Portability: Low; while the Hydra's Spine is a vast and interesting setting, it is very nearly another setting entirely. Information from Eta-13 expeditions might show up in otherwise unrelated material, but otherwise the task force is really only useful in stories set in the Hydra's Spine.
Review: These stories, while on the surface very reminiscent of Stargate SG-1 were still really entertaining. I really hope that this story continues after the contest.
Rank: NA

+ Challenge Accepted
– hide block

Team: Challenge Accepted
Entries: 1 SCP, 1 Format (Marshall, Carter and Dark Limited), 0 tales, 0 AARs, 0 edited inclusions
Qualification: No
Designation: Pi-51 "Art Critics"
Class: Tracking
Mission: Monitoring the anart scene
Portability: Average; the wheelhouse is pretty broad, but the low quality of the work and sparsity of information about the task force makes reusing it rather unattractive.
Review: The English was sufficiently poor that it was very difficult to read these pieces, and I don't really have an assessment of them beyond that.
Rank: NA

+ The Notos Jazz and Blues Experience
– hide block

Team: The Notos Jazz and Blues Experience
Entries: 1 SCP, 1 GOI format (Church of the Broken God — Clockwork Orthodoxy), 3 tales, 1 AAR, 0 edited inclusions. I think that SCP-2474 was the best contest SCP and that Exploration Log 2474.1 was the best AAR.
Qualification: Yes
Designation: MTF Rho-19 "Cytherians"
Class: Undercover
Mission: Infiltrate the New Shambala Venus Colony in order to contain or neutralize SCP-2474
Portability: Very low; this team's mission was very specific, they are in the far future relative to most Foundation-verse stories, and the task force was destroyed at the conclusion of the series.
Review: This was just an amazing science fiction story. It was beautiful, evocative, and flawlessly crafted. Manu-13 is one of the best characters to come out this wiki, ever.
Rank: 1st

+ Team Basic
– hide block

Team: Team Basic
Entries: 1 SCP, 2 GOI formats (Marshall Carter and Dark Limited and a Manna Charitable Foundation format screw), 4 tales, 1 AAR, and 1 edited inclusion. This team had the other AAR that wasn't what I was expecting from the contest requirements and they were one of the three teams that used a modified GOI format.
Qualification: Yes
Designation: MTF Kappa-10 "Skynet"
Class: Esoteric
Mission: Artificial Intelligence cyber-operations
Portability: Low; the task force's mission is fairly specific and the technical aspects of the visual style are potentially challenging.
Review: This was a very slick presentation that clearly took a lot of work, but ultimately the story told in Hello World was extremely trope-laden and pedestrian, and certainly didn't live up to the potential of artificially intelligent protagonists.
Rank: 7th

+ Evolved from Naturally Occurring Gears, Levers and Pulleys
– hide block

Team: Evolved from Naturally Occurring Gears, Levers and Pulleys
Entries: 1 SCP (deleted; not reviewed), 0 GOI formats, 2 tales, 1 AAR, 0 edited inclusions
Qualification: No
Designation: MTF Stigma-9 "Evolved from Naturally Occurring Gears, Levers and Pulleys"; this was one of two teams to not use the standard Greek alphanumeric designation. I think this nickname is way too long to actually be usable.
Class: Undercover
Mission: Covert operations involving the Church of the Broken God.
Portability: Low; the focus on the single GOI is limiting and the nickname is too long to easily use in dialog.
Review: This team's entries concentrated on Operation Hippodrome, a covert operation intended to feed false intelligence of a destabilizing nature to the CotB. The story felt incompletely developed.
Rank: NA

I felt that while there were two teams that I felt were very clearly 1st and 2nd place, and four teams that I felt had mostly missed the mark, ranking 3rd through 7th was difficult and these teams are all really very close (to the extent that I considered saying that 3rd place was a five-way tie, but this seemed like a copout).
